why: ROLLBACK. Facts (each sentence below is one of the claims): Claim 1: canary /search p99 is more than 5x the stable /search p99 (651 ms vs 61 ms). Claim 2: 18 canary /search requests exceeded 500 ms, while no stable request on any path exceeded 400 ms (stable max is 343 ms). Claim 3: there were zero 5xx responses on either version and all 18 slow canary /search responses returned HTTP 200. Claim 4: those 18 slow responses occur in 11 of the 12 ten-second buckets of the test, from t=3.18s to t=113.3s. Claim 5: canary /search latency is bimodal - the fast cluster maxes at 190 ms, the slow cluster starts at 633 ms, and nothing falls between 200 ms and 600 ms. Claim 6: /browse and /checkout show no canary regression - canary max latency is less than or equal to stable max latency on both paths. Claim 7: the slow cluster is 2.47% of canary /search requests and 0.76% of all canary requests. Judgement: version 1.1 has a reproducible ~650 ms slow path on /search that version 1.0 does not have anywhere in the log; because it is spread over the whole 120 s (Claim 4) it is not a warmup or restart artifact, and because it is a clean bimodal split with an empty gap (Claim 5) it looks like a distinct code path (e.g. a cache miss or fallback branch) rather than scheduling noise. The dashboard hides this because p50 and p95 are unchanged and the per-path regression only shows in /search p99. Judgement on blast radius: the defect is isolated to /search (Claim 6) and causes no errors (Claim 3), so this is not a customer-facing outage; but at 25% of traffic it already affects 2.47% of searches (Claim 7), and promoting to 100% would put every search request on that code path instead of one pod in four, so the count of ~650 ms searches would grow roughly fourfold. Judgement: a 10x search tail regression with a known-good 1.0 still running is worth diagnosing before promotion, so roll back rather than promote.
